details: An Object is a distinct tangible item created for a purpose.
A Material is the physical substance used to construct an object.
One object can be made from multiple materials (e.g., tumbler made of glass, steel, or plastic).
One material can make many objects (e.g., wood used for chairs, doors, rulers, tables).
experiments_or_examples: Grouping classroom objects by material type in Table 6.1

details: Lustre: Shiny appearance characteristic of metals (gold, copper, aluminum). Non-lustrous materials include wood and paper.
Hardness: Hard materials resist compression/scratching (iron, stone); soft materials compress easily (sponge, wax).
Solubility: Soluble substances dissolve completely in water (salt, sugar); insoluble substances remain undissolved (sand, chalk, sawdust).
experiments_or_examples: Stirring salt, sand, and chalk in water tumblers to observe solubility

details: Transparent: Light passes completely; objects seen clearly (clear glass, clean water, air).
Translucent: Light passes partially; objects seen blurred (butter paper, frosted glass, oily paper).
Opaque: Light cannot pass; objects cannot be seen (cardboard, wood, metals).
experiments_or_examples: Looking at a light source through glass, butter paper, and cardboard

branches.theme: 6.3 Definition of Matter and Historical Context

details: Matter is anything that possesses mass and occupies space (volume).
All physical materials (solids, liquids, gases) are matter.
Historical metallurgy: Ancient text 'Rasaratnasamuchchaya' notes crucibles were crafted from clay and iron ('Upadanam bhavettasya mrittika lohameva cha').
experiments_or_examples: Demonstrating that air in a balloon occupies space and adds mass
